The individual declarations are each legal; the 65535-byte row budget is a dialect-level composite limit, so this is a diagnostics gap (CREATE fails naming no field), not a declared-contract violation. Family serial note for the engine seat: this is one of four driver-sql cards queued this round (#11535 #11541 #11550 #11565, plus blocked #11431) — shared hot files around `createColumn`/schema-sync, so fold-or-serial must be answered explicitly under the five gates at dispatch.

Siblings this round: #11635 at `mapAggregateFunc` **12786** / lowering **7741**; #11550 at the dialect getters **4196-4208** + tables **4476** / **4584**. Disjoint.

⚠️ **The card's own reason for not fixing this in #11431 was that `initObjects` is "a hot region that sibling cards are working in". Re-measured: it is not hot now** — no open PR touches this file at all. That blocker has cleared, which is why this card is dispatchable today.

⚠️ **Read-coupling with #11550** (same round): it widens `isMysql` to recognise more knex client spellings. A MySQL-only pre-flight is **selected by** that getter, so which connections your check fires on depends on its landing. Additive, so no flip expected — but ⛔ do not edit the getters; they are #11550's region.

## What is settled, and what is not

**Settled** (the card's measurement, live MySQL 8.0.46, utf8mb4 / InnoDB / DYNAMIC): InnoDB caps the **sum** of a row's declared byte widths at 65535, independent of the per-column `varchar` ceiling. `16 x varchar(1024)` fails; `15` creates. `65 x varchar(255)` fails; `64` creates. Postgres has no equivalent (it TOASTs) — **MySQL-only**.

**Settled**: this is worth fixing because the server's error names **no field and no declaration**. It says "change some columns to TEXT or BLOBs" about a table the author described entirely in metadata. Sixteen fields at `maxLength: 1024` is not exotic, and an AI authoring a metadata app has no reason to suspect a cumulative limit exists.

**Not settled — the card is explicit it is "not prescribing"**, and this is the real work:

- a **pre-flight** at the call site that sums declared widths before issuing DDL and refuses naming the widest offenders; or
- an **`ER_TOO_BIG_ROWSIZE` translator** alongside `explainUnkeyableTextColumn`.

The card argues pre-flight is the better shape (it can name **every** contributing field; the post-hoc translator only knows the table failed). ⚠️ Treat that as a **PM-relayed suggestion, not a ruling** — measure and decide, and say which you chose and why. Two things worth weighing that the card does not:

1. A pre-flight must compute the same byte arithmetic MySQL does (charset bytes-per-char, the length prefix, per-row overhead). Getting it *wrong in the strict direction* refuses an object the server would have accepted — which is the contract change flagged above. Getting it wrong in the lax direction just means the server still refuses, with today's bad message.
2. The translator cannot over-refuse **by construction**, because it only speaks after the server has already refused. That asymmetry is worth naming in whichever direction you go.

⚠️ **`explainUnkeyableTextColumn` (#11374) is the in-repo precedent for exactly this shape** — a driver-side diagnostic that translates an unactionable MySQL refusal into one naming the declarations at fault. Read it before designing; matching its idiom is worth more than inventing a second one.

## Scope note carried from the card

No platform object is near the limit today (widest declared string bound anywhere is 2000; no object carries more than six such fields). ⛔ This is about **authored apps**, so do not expect an in-repo fixture to reproduce it — you will need to construct one, and live MySQL is available in this container (⛔ check first, start if down, configure to CI parity).

## ACCEPT — PR #11792

Reviewer of record: `domain:engine` seat, `huangyiirene`, session `session_01VK8rFDtg8eREaxBGX99Csn`. Checked against the diff. ⛔ Landing held pending my CI read — last section.

### ⭐ The card's preferred direction was wrong, and the measurement that kills it is decisive

The card argued for a **pre-flight** and I relayed that, adding only that a wrong-in-the-strict-direction pre-flight would be a contract change. The dev chose the **translator** instead and measured four things that make that the right call — the fourth on its own settles it:

1. **The charset multiplier is the SCHEMA's, not the metadata's.** `64 x varchar(1024)` is refused on utf8mb4 and **creates on latin1**. A pre-flight hardcoding 4 bytes/char over-refuses by 4×.
2. **The length prefix moves at a 255-BYTE payload boundary, not 255 characters.** utf8mb4 `varchar(63)` = 253 bytes; `varchar(64)` = 258.
3. **The null bitmap counts.** `163 x varchar(100)` is refused nullable and **creates as NOT NULL** — same declared widths, different verdict.
4. ⭐ **DECISIVE — there is a SECOND independent limit behind the same error code.** InnoDB's per-page limit ("Row size too large (> 8126)") refuses **40 ordinary fields at `maxLength: 63`** through this driver — about **one sixth** of the 65535 budget. **A 65535-byte pre-flight waves that straight through** and hands the author exactly the unactionable error this card exists to remove.

So the pre-flight would not merely risk over-refusing — it would **under-refuse the common case while looking authoritative**. That is worse than the defect.

And the card's stated reason for preferring pre-flight — *"the post-hoc translator only knows the table failed"* — is **measured false at this call site**: the catch sits inside `initObjects`' own loop with `obj.fields` and `keyedColumns` in scope, so it names every contributing field exactly as a pre-flight would. The translator gets the pre-flight's whole benefit and, by construction, cannot over-refuse — it speaks only after the server has already refused.

I relayed a preference; the dev replaced it with a measurement. That is the transaction working.

### Form and scope

| Check | Reading |
|---|---|
| Path surface | ✅ 3 files. No governed path. |
| Regions | ✅ `initObjects` **8870-8919** and the diagnostic neighbourhood **13163+**, beside `explainUnkeyableTextColumn` as briefed. Plus a 14-line local `interface RowWidthContribution` above the class at 3941 — outside my declared region but benign, and textually clear of #11550's getters. |
| Sibling fence | ✅ **zero** dialect-getter reads added — and by design, not by luck: `ER_TOO_BIG_ROWSIZE` is a MySQL code, so the translator needs no dialect predicate and the diff never approaches #11550's region. |
| No over-refusal | ✅ nothing accepted before is refused now — pinned, see below. |
| Tier | ✅ unchanged: the contract-change risk I flagged (refusing what MySQL would accept) is structurally absent from the chosen shape. |

### Evidence

**Boundaries re-measured *through the driver*, not copied from the card's raw-SQL table** — and they moved, because the driver adds `id varchar(255)` plus the audit timestamps: `maxLength: 255` → **63 creates / 64 refused** where raw SQL was 64/65. The `id` column eats one field's worth. Both sides of both boundaries pinned live. Copying the card's numbers would have produced a pin that is off by exactly one field.

**Reverse verification: 9 of 10 red**, mutation proven on disk by marker count 4→0 *before* any result was read, trap-restored. ⭐ And the one that stayed green is the right one — **the no-over-refusal pin, which asserts unchanged behaviour and must be green in both directions.** Noticing that a correct ablation leaves exactly that pin standing is the difference between running an ablation and reading one.

**A claim was dropped rather than pinned**: `varcharPackLength` at a payload of exactly 255 bytes. Such a column is never stored off-page, so InnoDB's page limit binds at ~31 columns and *neither* limit can discriminate 256 from 257 bytes. The implementation follows the documented rule, the comment says so, and the boundary is bracketed by measurement at 252 and 256. ⭐ **An unmeasurable claim did not get a pin** — the alternative is a green nobody can interpret.

**The `FieldType.options`-driven pin** asserts the width mirror agrees with `createColumn` for **every** field type the spec declares, so a new spec type joins the pin automatically rather than silently escaping it.

Lane conformance promise: 45/0/0 before and after, with the before taken on a reverted tree under a trap-restore.

### Declared scope addition — accepted

The **`ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN`** site is wrapped as well as `CREATE TABLE`: same defect, sibling call site twenty lines down, one shared helper, two catches. The dev's argument is right and worth keeping: it is **the more reachable half in a living app**, where a field added to an already-wide object is refused by the width of columns nobody is touching. Declared in the PR body, not slipped in.

### Follow-up — a real bug the pin found

**#11794**: `richtext` is emitted as `varchar(255)` while its `markdown`/`html` siblings get `TEXT` — it is absent from `createColumn`'s text-family case and falls through to the catch-all, so a rich-text body over 255 characters is refused on MySQL (`ER_DATA_TOO_LONG`) and Postgres (`22001`). `code`, `signature` and `qrcode` share the fall-through.

⭐ This was **found by the FieldType agreement pin**, not by inference — which is precisely what that pin was built to do, on its first run. Duplicate-searched before filing (#11431 is the string family, #11374 is keyed text), unassigned and unlabelled for triage, and cross-referenced for serialisation against the two adjacent cards.

### On the timing

This card ran ~112 minutes, past the ~105 max I had recorded. It was alive and productive throughout, and no death call was made — which is the second time today that holding to "overrun is a probe threshold, never a death threshold" was the right read. The probe I sent at ~78 minutes cost one message; declaring it dead would have cost a second agent in a worktree that was, at that moment, measuring InnoDB page limits.

### ⛔ Landing held

Verdict ACCEPT. I have not yet read this PR's check runs; entry needs **every** check green, not the `required` subset. ⚠️ Two sibling PRs on this same file (#11783, #11785) are also unlanded — their hunks are textually disjoint from these, so the merge queue can order them freely, but each will re-run against whatever base it gets.
